primary_meaning: Belief is most commonly understood not as a symbolic image but as faith: accepting the truth of God’s revelation and personally trusting, relying upon, and committing oneself to God—especially to Jesus Christ—for salvation.
primary_basis: John 3:16–18 — believing in the Son is contrasted with unbelief and associated with eternal life.
John 6:28–29, 35, 40 — believing in Christ is portrayed as coming to him and receiving life.
John 20:30–31 — the Gospel’s signs are recorded so that readers may believe Jesus is the Christ and have life in his name.
Acts 16:30–31 — belief in the Lord Jesus is presented as the response leading to salvation.
Romans 4:3–5, 18–24 — Abraham’s belief exemplifies trusting God’s promise and is reckoned as righteousness.
Romans 10:9–13 — heart-belief and confession of Jesus as Lord are associated with salvation.
Galatians 2:16 — justification is associated with faith in Jesus Christ rather than works of the law.
Hebrews 11:1, 6 — faith entails confidence in what is hoped for and trust in God’s existence and faithfulness.
James 2:14–26 — living faith is distinguished from bare intellectual assent by its resulting actions.

alternatives.meaning: Belief as intellectual assent: accepting a proposition as true, without necessarily implying personal trust, obedience, or saving commitment.
basis: James 2:19 explicitly describes demons as believing that God is one, showing that belief can denote factual assent without saving faith.
John 12:42–43 describes people who believed in Jesus yet would not openly confess him.
Acts 8:13, 18–24 has often been used in discussions of belief that may be superficial or deficient.

alternatives.meaning: Belief as allegiance or loyal commitment to Jesus as Lord, emphasizing fidelity and embodied obedience more than inward assent.
basis: Romans 10:9 connects belief with confessing Jesus as Lord.
John 3:36 can be translated or understood in terms of believing in versus disobeying the Son.
Romans 1:5 and 16:26 speak of the “obedience of faith.”
Philippians 2:9–11 presents confession of Jesus’ lordship in royal and covenantal terms.

alternatives.meaning: Belief as divinely enabled faith or a gift of grace rather than primarily an autonomous human decision.
basis: John 6:44, 65 stresses the Father’s enabling of those who come to Christ.
Acts 13:48 associates belief with appointment to eternal life.
Ephesians 2:8–9 is frequently cited in debates over whether faith itself is included in God’s gift.
Philippians 1:29 speaks of belief in Christ as something granted.

alternatives.meaning: Belief as confident expectation that prayer, confession, or inner certainty will produce a desired outcome, especially healing or material blessing.
basis: Mark 11:22–24 is frequently interpreted as requiring unwavering belief in prayer.
Matthew 17:20 links faith with apparently impossible outcomes.
James 5:15 speaks of the prayer of faith in connection with healing.

notes: There is broad Christian consensus that “belief” centrally involves faith or trust, particularly trust in God and Christ. There is no single settled symbolic interpretation because the biblical words translated “believe” normally function as direct theological and relational language rather than as a conventional symbol. Disagreement concerns whether particular occurrences emphasize factual assent, personal trust, loyalty, obedience, divine enablement, or some combination of these.
